en: Preface to the Original Edition of the Four Pure Land Sutras My friend Wei Moshen (Yuan) of Shaoyang was profoundly versed in the religious teachings. In his later years, he devoted himself exclusively to the practice of the Pure Land.

In the spring of the sixth year, he dispatched a letter from Qinyou to inquire after my welfare and sent me a hand-copied manuscript of the four sutras, accompanied by a preface. The letter stated: "The Old..."
Fellow practitioners of our generation, in these times of hardship, all conditioned phenomena are unreliable.

Only this Dharma that transcends the three realms is accomplished through the vow-power of our Buddha. If you simply prepare a single-minded resolve, you will ultimately ascend to the nine grades of rebirth.

Furthermore, this Dharma gate of mindfulness of the Buddha universally benefits those of the three faculties; regardless of whether one is wise or foolish, male or female, all may practice it. If one can...

It has been carved into woodblocks and circulated; the benefit [thereof] is no small matter. You, my son, must exert yourself in its practice without slackening. I have respectfully received these instructions.
However, the original manuscript was recorded by Master Moshen during his illness and contains many errors, such as those of "fish and pig" (i.e., miswritten characters).

Since my collection of books is meager, and I dwell in a humble place at the edge of the sea where there are no fine editions available for comparison, I have engraved and revised it repeatedly over two seasons, beginning only now.
When the work was successfully completed and the collated edition had been finalized, I recorded its origins at the beginning of the volume.
All the prefaces to the sutras were signed with the name Chengguan; this was, in fact, my secret dharma name.
A Humble Record by the Lay Practitioner Zhou Yipu of Xiangtan,
on an Auspicious Day in the Second Month of Autumn in the Year of Wuma (the 8th Year of the Xianfeng Reign):
General Preface to the Four Pure Land Sutras.
The Imperially Selected Records of Sayings, compiled by the Emperor Shizong Xianhuangdi, includes the imperial preface to the various sayings on the Pure Land by Master Lianchi,
which elucidates the principle of the unification of the Zen school and the Pure Land.
When Emperor Gaozong Chun performed his southern tour, he personally visited Yunqi, where he offered incense and paid homage to the Buddha.
His imperial poem contains the line, "The six characters from whence they come encompass the three vehicles. How magnificent!
The teaching of the Sage of the West has been received by the East.

The Sage then manifested and proclaimed them. Now, the Way of the King (the secular way) governs the world, while the Way of the Buddha transcends the world. Those who cling to outward traces perceive them as different;

those with perfectly functioning faculties perceive them as the same. Furthermore, within the Way that transcends the world, there are distinctions between the schools of Chan, Teaching, Vinaya, and Pure Land.
Those who value their own spiritual nature within and exclusively practice the Perfect and Sudden (the *yuan-dun*) belong to the school of the Teaching (*jiao*).

Those who look outwardly toward the various sages and seek to invoke the Buddha’s power through the power of their own mind belong to the Pure Land school (*jingtu*). Furthermore, there are those who look outwardly toward the various sages while valuing their own spiritual nature within;

this is the combined practice of the School and the Pure Land, which accelerates progress on the Path even more rapidly. As for the Vinaya (*lü*), it serves as the foundation for the Teaching, the School, and the Pure Land, yet it is not [one of them].

This is its ultimate consummation. Now, according to the religious teachings and the Vinaya, one must first resolve to attain enlightenment (*bodhicitta*), leave the household life as a celibate youth, and pass through many long kalpas from the First Stage (*prathamā bhūmi*) to the Tenth Stage (*daśamī bhūmi*) before being designated as one of Equal and Wondrous Enlightenment (*samyaksambuddha*).

Even without receiving a prediction (*vyākaraṇa*) from a Buddha, one attains Buddhahood on one's own. What kind of spiritual capacity (*indriya*) is this? It is simply a method for accomplishing the goal in a single lifetime. This is my Buddha Amitāyus.
World-Honored One, regarding the teaching of rebirth in the Pure Land, it is a horizontal transcendence of the triple world.

Compared to the vertical transcendence of the triple world, there is a difference as vast as heaven and earth in terms of difficulty and ease, and nearness and distance. This is what the Chan Master Yongming Shou meant when he said:
"With Chan but no Pure Land, nine out of ten go astray; with no Chan but the Pure Land, ten thousand who practice, ten thousand depart. With both Chan and the Pure Land...

Master T'u-t'ai was like a horned tiger. Master Yun-ch'i revitalized the Pure Land school by specializing in the propagation of the *Smaller Sukhāvatīvyūha Sūtra*, yet he failed to address the *Larger Sukhāvatīvyūha Sūtra*, the *Sūtra on the Visualization of the Buddha of Infinite Life*, and the "Universal Worthy’s Vows and Practices" chapter.
Now, if one does not read the *Larger Sukhāvatīvyūha Sūtra*, how can one know the vastness of Dharmākara’s ocean of vows during his stage of causal practice?
Profound. It does not follow the sequence of the perfection of the stage of fruition.

How else could one know the adornments of the World of Ultimate Bliss and the grades of the nine levels of rebirth? Once the great resolve has been awakened, the objects of contemplation are experienced directly.
Thereafter, one must ultimately rely upon the practice of holding the name. This does not mean that making vows and performing visualizations may be abandoned in favor of holding the name.

When the practice of holding the name reaches the state of single-mindedness without distraction, rebirth in the Pure Land is assured; only then does one take up residence in the *Universal Worthy’s Practices and Vows*.
By means of the ten great kings of vows, one encompasses the twenty-four vows of Amitāyus;

by making each vow continuous from moment to moment without interruption, and ensuring that the actions of body, speech, and mind are free from weariness, one encompasses the "single-mindedness without distraction" of the *Sukhāvatīvyūha Sūtra*.
Therefore, those who manifest in the forms of officials, elders, or lay devotees should recite these four sūtras and master them through diligent study.
After completing the recitation, one should act in accordance with the understanding gained. First, one must resolve to attain unsurpassed bodhicitta.
On a grand scale, this means vowing to sever boundless afflictions, to deliver inexhaustible sentient beings, to study immeasurable Dharma gates, and to realize the unsurpassed path of the Buddha.
On a more immediate scale, it involves extensively practicing generosity and making offerings to the Triple Gem. Much...

I have published Mahāyāna sūtras as well as various scriptures and treatises on the Pure Land, so that all monastic communities shall establish a separate Buddha-recitation hall outside the meditation hall.
This ensures that those who have left the household life will all attain rebirth in the Western Paradise, which is certainly a most favorable development.

However, even among laypeople in white robes, there are those who do not yet fully understand the meaning of "hearing the Dharma in the morning and dying in the evening"; if they were suddenly presented with these four scriptures, they might not necessarily accept or listen to them. Nevertheless...
Even those who doubt the Buddha or slander the Buddha plant the roots of faith; how much more so must it be for all wriggling and sentient beings, who surely all possess the Buddha-nature?
Now, the merit of exhorting and transforming a single person to achieve Buddhahood is immeasurable;

how then can one fathom the merit of exhorting and transforming dozens, hundreds, or even thousands, tens of thousands, millions, and billions of monks, leading them all to be reborn in the Western Land and attain Buddhahood? As an ancient worthy said:

Those who first deliver themselves and only thereafter deliver others are like the Tathāgatas appearing in the world; those who, unable yet to deliver themselves, first vow to deliver others are the Bodhisattvas who resolve their minds.

Thereafter, one closes the gate of seven days of mindfulness of the Buddha to seek single-mindedness without distraction, and again closes the gate of seven days of contemplation of the Buddha to seek direct vision of the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss, both its environment and its inhabitants. This is because...
Entry into the path must necessarily proceed through sequential cultivation before reaching perfect cultivation. Nothing is more perfect than the "Chapter on the Vows of Samantabhadra.
Therefore, it constitutes the ultimate destination of the Avataṃsaka Sūtra. This is the natural sequence and the fixed rule for practice;
thus, these four scriptures have been compiled together for wide circulation, so that all sentient beings may together ascend to perfect enlightenment.
In the fourth year of the Xianfeng era, the disciple of the Bodhisattva Precepts, Wei Chengguan, respectfully prefaces this collective translation of the *Sukhāvatīvyūha Sūtra*.
Master Lianchi set aside the *Longer Sukhāvatīvyūha* and the *Amitāyurdhyāna Sūtra*, and instead took the *Shorter Sukhāvatīvyūha* as his primary school. This was indeed...

This is already partial rather than complete. As for the *Fahui* (Collection of Dharma) from Yunqi Monastery, it published the long version of the *Amitābha Sūtra* and exclusively utilized the Wei translation;
furthermore, it claimed that the forty-eight vows have circulated throughout both ancient and modern times.

However, Vasubandhu Bodhisattva’s *Verses on the Infinite Life* already states that there are twenty-four chapters of vows, which shows that such was the case in the ancient manuscripts of the Western Regions. Therefore, the two translations by the Han and Wu periods [are incomplete].

Its core consists of twenty-four vows. From the Wei dynasty translation onward, these were elaborated and doubled; they became repetitive and redundant, with the preceding and succeeding sections being nearly identical.
Therefore, the Tang dynasty translation condensed them into forty-six vows, and the Song dynasty translation further condensed them into thirty-six vows.
These earlier versions did not circulate, nor do they circulate today. Furthermore, the "five pains and five burnings" are superfluous additions.

The subsequent verses are absent from the Tang dynasty translation of the *Ratnakūṭa-sūtra*. Consequently, the *Sukhāvatīvyūha-sūtra* has not been included in the daily liturgical recitations of the monastic communities until the present day.

This causes the Great Vow of our Buddha, the World-Honored One—which encompasses the ocean of fruition within the cause and reaches the source of the cause through the fruition—to remain unmanifest in the world.
Is this not indeed a profound regret for the teachings of the Pure Land scriptures? I have therefore carefully collated several translations to...

This scripture has been completed. There is not a single character that lacks its provenance; it is hoped that this may remedy the deficiencies of Yunqi [Zhuhong] and serve as an excellent foundational text for the Dharma gate.
Some might say: "Based on your separate edition of the sutra commentary, you imitate Yunqi’s *Amitābha Sūtra Commentary* by tracing every point back to the self-nature (*svabhāva*).
Yet, you do not fully grasp the essence of 'loving' (the Pure Land), nor do you transcend the Sahā world. As for those [treasures] made of crystal, musaragalva, and coral..."
Agate, gold, silver, precious jewel-trees, pavilions, necklaces, and celestial music—how could these have anything to do with the nature of one's own being?
Yet, why does the Sūtra speak so enthusiastically of the World of Ultimate Bliss? It is said: This is the natural manifestation of the Dharmakāya, Sambhogakāya, and Nirmāṇakāya.
The Sahā world is originally the thirteenth layer of the Flower Treasury World (*Kusumatalagarbha-lokadhātu*). Sentient beings...

Regarding what others viewed as mere pits, mounds, earth, and stones, the World-Honored One stepped upon them with his supernormal powers (*ṛddhi-pāda*), and the ground beneath his feet was transformed into a floor of lapis lazuli (*vaidūrya*).
Upon withdrawing his supernormal powers, it returned to its former state. This is the extraordinary response resulting from the causes and effects of a Buddha’s life.

All sentient beings possess the six sense faculties (*ṣaḍ-indriya*); possessing these six faculties entails the existence of the six objects (*ṣaḍ-viṣaya*) and the six bases (*ṣaḍ-āyatana*). Therefore, the eye desires the ultimate...
Regarding the colors of the world: the ears desire to exhaustively experience all sounds of the world; the tongue desires to exhaustively experience all flavors of the world;
the nose desires to exhaustively experience all fragrances of the world; the body desires to exhaustively experience all fine and smooth tactile sensations of the world;

and the mind desires to exhaustively experience all things that bring mental pleasure. Those who seek and obtain these [rewards] receive the meritorious retributions of the various devas, yet they do not realize that their celestial blessings will eventually be exhausted.
It is easy to fall away from it. Next is the Way of Humanity (*mānuṣa-yāna*). In the human way, one is enslaved by the physical body, wife, and children for a lifetime;

suffering and joy are intertwined. Furthermore, wealth and status drown a person, making it easy to enter the three miserable realms (*tri-durgati*). Such are the difficulties of remaining in the household.
Regarding the monastics who have left the household life, apart from the combined practice of Chan and Pure Land by Zhiyi and Yongming, all others merely claim to follow the Mahayana.
Yet, they wish to ascend from the first stage (*bhūmi*) to the tenth stage through the passage of long kalpas.
Furthermore, Bodhisattvas suffer from the delusion of being separated from the physical body; Yunmen, Qingtao, and the Fifth Patriarch Jie serve as precedents and warnings against this. This is so.

The vertical transcendence of the triple world is difficult to achieve. Therefore, the Great Sage, the Awakened King, took pity on sentient beings and, outside of the vertical transcendence of the triple world, established the method of horizontal transcendence of the triple world:
to fully realize the true within the deluded and to bring provisional means back to the ultimate reality.

To scoop up the waters of the great ocean to obtain the finest essence (*sarpis-manda*); to transform the vast earth into pure gold; with a single cry, to awaken the magnificent name of myriad virtues.
Within the hearts of every person dwells Amitāyus Buddha, who emits light that shakes the earth. By opening a speck of dust, one finds the scroll; from within one’s own robes, one obtains the pearl.

Thus one comes to know that desire is the root of suffering, yet desire is also the root of the Way. If joy does not reach its ultimate limit, weariness will not arise; once weariness reaches its peak...
If one does not reach the ultimate, one cannot escape the three realms. Thus one must aspire, thus one must choose and take up, and thus one must transcend.
Only after this may one perform a single prostration, a single visualization, or a single recitation of the name. In every thought-moment, one looks up to Amitābha as to a compassionate father;
like one in the throes of illness calling out to Heaven, or like one fleeing a prison toward a precious sanctuary. Even if the mind is not yet single-minded—nevertheless, [one must proceed].

This is indeed possible. Otherwise, if one maintains the Great Name with the mouth while the mind hankers after worldly pleasures, yet desires to ultimately transcend the three realms—would this not be most difficult?
The Bodhisattva Precept Disciple Wei Chengguan respectfully prefaces the *Sūtra of Immeasurable Life*.

Thus have I heard. At one time the Buddha was staying at Rājagṛha on Vulture Peak Mountain, together with a great assembly of twelve hundred and fifty bhikṣus; all of whom were great śrāvakas, well-known to the public, namely:
the Venerable Kauṇḍinya, the Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana, the Venerable Śāriputra, and the Venerable Kāśyapa.
Venerable Ānanda and other great disciples served as the leaders [of the assembly] (the names of the various arhats are recorded in some versions using Sanskrit and in others using Chinese;

here, only five venerable ones are listed by way of illustration for the rest). Furthermore, Samantabhadra Bodhisattva, Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva, Maitreya Bodhisattva, and all the bodhisattvas of the Bhadrakalpa all came to assemble. All these bodhisattvas...
Possessing immeasurable vows and practices, planting the roots of all virtues, and endowed with every merit, he employs skillful means and travels through the buddha-fields.
He manifests universally to make offerings to all buddhas and to transform and guide sentient beings.

Having realized the characteristics of sentient beings and penetrated the nature of all dharmas, he is like a skilled illusionist who conjures the forms of men, women, and so forth; yet within those forms, there is truly nothing to be apprehended. Thus he enters [the state of non-attainment].
Through the samādhis of emptiness, wishlessness, and signlessness, they are able to fully realize the dhāraṇīs and immeasurable hundreds of thousands of samādhis.

Abiding in the gates of profound concentration, they behold all the immeasurable Buddhas of the present. Within a single thought-moment, they travel throughout all Buddha-lands, discerning the languages of sentient beings and regarding them with compassion as if they were their own kin. They vow to accomplish the immeasurable merits of all Buddhas and transcend...

The stages of all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas. (This section praising the merit of the bodhisattvas is absent from the Song translation; here it follows the four other translations, with redundant phrasing omitted.
Furthermore, there were five hundred bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs; seven thousand pure upāsakas; five hundred pure upāsikās; eight hundred thousand devaputras of the desire realm;
seven hundred thousand devaputras of the form realm; and [devas of] the Universal Purity [heaven].
Six hundred thousand sons of heaven and one hundred million Brahmās—such an immeasurable multitude gathered together like clouds at once.

(These nine phrases are not found in any other translation; they were added from the Chinese version. For this sutra universally benefits those of the three capacities—superior, middling, and inferior—it is appropriate to list first the ordinary and holy beings, men and women, and the fourfold assembly of lay and ordained followers, thereby representing the specific audience.

At that time, the World-Honored One’s majestic radiance was brilliant and dazzling, like a mass of molten gold, and like a pure, bright mirror, with its reflections clearly manifest both within and without. (Five phrases)

(Compiled using the translations of both Wei and Tang dynasties. A great radiance appeared, manifesting in hundreds and thousands of transformations. (These eight characters are added based on the Han and Wu translations. Venerable Ānanda then reflected to himself:
"Today the World-Honored One’s faculties are joyful and at ease; his countenance is pure and radiant;
this majestic jewel-adorned land is magnificent, such as I have never seen since time immemorial. How fortunate I am to behold him, giving rise to a sense of rare wonder. (The above)

[The second section follows; it incorporates both the Wei and Han translations. He immediately rose from his seat, bared his right shoulder, knelt with his right knee on the ground, joined his palms, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One, today you have entered the Great Samādhi of Quiescence. You abide in the most extraordinary and vast Dharma; you abide in the supreme path where all Buddhas dwell.
Are you mindful of the Buddhas of the past and future? Or are you mindful of the Buddhas currently residing in other directions?
We pray that you will explain this, for the benefit of all. (The above three lines are adapted from various translations. At that time, the World-Honored One...
He addressed Ānanda, saying: "Excellent, excellent, Ānanda! Out of compassion and for the benefit of all sentient beings, you have been able to inquire about such a subtle and profound meaning.

This question of yours now surpasses the merit of making offerings to the arhats and pratyekabuddhas throughout a single world-system, or the merit of practicing charity toward the devas, humans, insects, and crawling creatures for the duration of many kalpas."
The merit of this is hundreds of thousands of millions of times greater than that of those who merely move [the body].
Why is this? Because all future devas, humans, and all sentient beings shall, by virtue of your inquiry, attain liberation. (This section is based on the Han and Wu translations.

Ānanda, the appearance of a Tathāgata in the world is difficult to encounter and difficult to behold; it is like the udumbara flower, appearing only once in a great while. What you have now asked will bring great benefit to many.
"Excellent! I shall expound it for you, to enlighten and transform all beings. (The final seven phrases are from the Wei translation, with words and phrasing drawn from various versions.
The Buddha told Ānanda: "In the distant past, immeasurable, inconceivable, and incalculable kalpas ago..."
There was a Buddha who appeared in the world, named Lokeśvararāja Tathāgata, who remained in the world for forty-two kalpas.

(The original text traces back from Lokeśvararāja Buddha to fifty-two Buddhas of the *sthiti-kalpa*, aligning with Dīpaṃkara Buddha as the beginning and end; both the Tang and Song translations count upward in reverse order, whereas the Han and Wu translations count downward in forward order.

Some argue that since Dīpaṃkara was the teacher who bestowed the prophecy upon Śākyamuni, it would be illogical for Dharmākara to have first resolved his mind [for enlightenment] after the fifty-third Buddha; others argue that many ancient Buddhas shared the same names, making it impossible to determine the correct sequence, and furthermore, past Buddhas are too numerous to count, so this is not a scriptural matter.)

Because these matters are related to our friendship, I have omitted them here; I shall begin instead from the time of the Tathāgata Lokeśvararāja to quell all doubts and disputes. Within that Buddha’s teaching, there was a bhikṣu named Dharmākara.
He had originally been a king who, upon hearing the Buddha preach the Dharma, immediately conceived the unsurpassed, true, and right aspiration for the Way.
He abandoned his kingdom and renounced his royal status to become a śramaṇa. His wisdom and valor were such that none could surpass him. He then went before the Tathāgata Lokeśvararāja.

He prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, joined his palms toward the Buddha, and addressed the Buddha, saying: (Below this point, various editions contain verses, either in four-character or five-character lines.)

Or seven-character lines (these are absent only in the Wu translation; here I follow the Wu translation): "So be it, World-Honored One. I have already resolved to attain unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment."
"I pray that the Buddha will extensively proclaim for me the adornments of the pure lands of all buddhas, so that I may attain peerless awakening in this world and realize great bodhi.
Then, the World-Honored One, King of Sovereign Power, spoke to the bhikṣu Dharmākara: "Regarding the adornment of buddha-lands..."
"You should restrain yourself. The bhikṣu addressed the Buddha, "This meaning is vast and profound; it is not within my sphere of experience.

I only pray that the World-Honored One will expound it for me. At that time, the Buddha Lokeśvararāja, knowing his high intelligence and his deep and broad aspirations, immediately expounded in detail upon two hundred and ten billion buddha-fields, including the good and evil of devas and humans, and the coarseness or subtlety of those lands.

In accordance with their mental aspirations, [the Buddha] manifested everything for them. At that time, having heard what the Buddha taught regarding the adornment and purification of buddha-fields, those bhikṣus beheld them all and gave rise to unsurpassed and most excellent vows; their minds became tranquil and their resolve was free from attachment.
Having cultivated merit and made great vows, he adorned himself with these attainments for five kalpas. He then went before the Buddha Lokeśvararāja and said:

"I now practice for the sake of the bodhisattva path, desiring that when I later become a buddha, among the countless buddhas of the eight directions, above, and below, my wisdom, light, and merit shall be preeminent among all those buddha-fields."

"Is it possible to attain it? The Buddha said, "It is like the great ocean: if a single person were to measure it with a peck-measure, even after the passing of kalpas, one might still reach its bottom.
If a person seeks the Way with a sincere heart, what wish could they not obtain? (The above twelve lines are from the Wei translation, with selections from the Wu translation.)
At that time, the Bhikṣu Dharmākara bowed his head to the Buddha’s feet, circumambulated the Buddha three times, and stood with palms joined, addressing the Buddha:
"World-Honored One, I have already undertaken the practices for the pure adornment of a buddha-land; I pray only that you will deign to hear and examine them.
First Vow: If, when I attain buddhahood, there should be even the name of the three evil realms in my land—whether it be hell-beings, hungry ghosts, or animals—"
[If] I should attain Buddhahood, yet there be those who hear my name and do not take birth [in my land], until then may I not achieve perfect enlightenment. The second vow:
If, when I attain Buddhahood, the gods and humans in my land are born solely by transformation (*upapāduka*), with no birth from a womb and no women;

and if women from other lands who wish to be born in my country, at the end of their lives, immediately transform into male bodies and come to my realm to be born within lotus flowers—[if this be not so, may I not attain enlightenment].
I vow that upon attaining Buddhahood, all shall behold me. If this were not so, I would not take perfect enlightenment. Third Vow:

Suppose, when I attain Buddhahood, the gods and humans in my land should have differing forms and colors, such that some are handsome and others ugly, and they do not all possess golden bodies and the thirty-two marks of a Great Man—if this were so, I would not take perfect enlightenment.
Fourth Vow: Suppose, when I attain Buddhahood, the gods and humans in my land should not all be able to know [the thoughts of one another]—if this were so, I would not take perfect enlightenment.

Fifth Vow: Should I attain Buddhahood, may all beings in my land not realize perfect enlightenment if they do not possess the knowledge of past lives, reaching down to the ability to know the events of hundreds of thousands of billions of nayutas of kalpas.

Sixth Vow: Should I attain Buddhahood, may all gods and humans in my land not realize perfect enlightenment if they do not possess the divine eye, reaching down to the ability to see hundreds of thousands of billions of nayutas of Buddha-lands. [Seventh Vow: Should I attain Buddhahood, within my land...

If, when I attain Buddhahood, the devas and humans in my land should not obtain the divine ear such that they hear, even down to the extent of hundreds of thousands of billions of nayutas of Buddhas preaching the Dharma, and fail to receive and uphold it all, may I not attain perfect enlightenment. This is the seventh vow.

Furthermore, if, when I attain Buddhahood, the devas and humans in my land should not obtain the knowledge of others' minds such that they know, even down to the extent of the sentient beings within hundreds of thousands of billions of nayutas of Buddha-lands, may I not attain perfect enlightenment. This is the eighth vow.

"Regarding the mental vow: I shall not attain perfect enlightenment if, upon my becoming a Buddha, the gods and humans in my land are unable to attain the power of spiritual travel (*ṛddhi-pāda*), such that in a single thought-moment they cannot, at the very least, traverse hundreds of thousands of billions of *nayuta* Buddha-lands.
This is the eighth vow. Regarding the ninth vow: If, upon my becoming a Buddha, the gods and humans in my land should not..."

The tenth vow: If, when I attain Buddhahood, the devas and humans in my land do not all obtain a broad and long tongue and skillfulness in preaching the Dharma, may I not attain perfect enlightenment.
Furthermore, those who dwell in the extinction of outflows (*āsravakṣaya*) and have attained the certainty of realizing great *nirvāṇa* shall not take [this] as their formal awakening.
Eleventh Vow: If, when I attain Buddhahood, my eloquence were not unimpeded, I would not take perfect enlightenment.

Furthermore, if my radiance were limited and did not pervade hundreds of thousands of billions of nayutas of Buddha-lands, surpassing the radiance of all other Buddhas, and if sentient beings of the ten directions who touched this light did not have their bodies and minds become supple and soft, and their karmic defilements eliminated, I would not take perfect enlightenment. My life...
Twelfth Vow: If, upon my attaining Buddhahood, there should be those who do not all attain rebirth in my land, may I not attain perfect enlightenment. Thirteenth Vow:
If, upon my attaining Buddhahood, my lifespan should have a finite limit, even as short as a hundred thousand *koṭi-nayuta* kalpas, may I not attain perfect enlightenment.
Fourteenth Vow: If, upon my attaining Buddhahood, there should be a measurable number of śrāvakas in my land, even as many as three thousand great...

If all sentient beings in a thousandfold world-system were to become pratyekabuddhas and together calculate for hundreds of thousands of kalpas, yet were unable to know their number, I shall not attain perfect enlightenment.

This is the fourteenth vow. If, when I attain Buddhahood, the lifespan of the devas and humans in my land shall also be like that of the Buddha, being immeasurable and without limit, such that they shall forever be free from birth and death—except as they manifest long or short lifespans by virtue of their own original vows—I shall not attain perfect enlightenment. This is the fourteenth vow.
[If this were not so,] I would not attain perfect enlightenment. The fifteenth vow:
If, upon my attaining Buddhahood, the gods and humans in my land do not all possess infinite radiance that illuminates all Buddha-lands, may I not attain perfect enlightenment.
The sixteenth vow: If, upon my attaining Buddhahood, my name is not universally heard throughout the worlds of the ten directions, [and is not known by immeasurable...]
Seventeenth Vow: "If, upon my attaining Buddhahood, all the Buddhas do not fully praise and extol my name, may I not attain perfect enlightenment.
Furthermore, if sentient beings of the ten directions, upon hearing my name, should resolve their minds on Bodhi and believe and rejoice with a sincere heart..."

If, when those who desire to be born in my land—even those who, at the moment of death, seek birth with ten recitations—do not see me and the great assembly surrounding me appear before them, may I not attain perfect enlightenment;
except for those who have committed the five heinous crimes or have slandered the true Dharma. The Eighteenth Vow:
If, when I attain Buddhahood, the multitudes of bodhisattvas from the Buddha-lands of other quarters who come to be born in my land do not ultimately...
He shall surely reach the stage of being born only once more before Buddhahood (*ekajātipratibaddha*).

Except for his original vow to freely transform those he guides and to travel throughout all Buddha-lands to deliver all sentient beings while practicing the bodhisattva path—even if born in other lands—he shall never undergo the sufferings of the three miserable realms and shall never lose his roots of goodness. If this were not so, may I not attain perfect enlightenment. This is the nineteenth vow. If...

they have no wealth or treasures, yet they worry about wealth and treasures; they have no kinsmen or retinues, yet they worry about kinsmen and retinues. Only when these things are suddenly obtained do they find peace."
Furthermore, there is anxiety regarding impermanence: fire, water, thieves, and enemies or creditors burn, flood, plunder, and seize one’s possessions day and night, never ceasing.
